author: EmuCore - Hub
title: RPCS3 Integrates OpenXR for Virtual Reality Headset and Controller Support
summary: A new OpenXR backend brings VR support to RPCS3 on Windows and Linux, allowing players to use VR headsets for immersive rendering and VR controllers for PlayStation Move emulation.
heroAlt: A close-up of a PlayStation 3 console and a DualShock 3 controller on a dark surface.

blocks.text: The Challenge of VR in Emulation

Emulating the PlayStation 3's complex architecture is already a significant task, but providing an immersive VR experience adds another layer of difficulty. Previously, RPCS3 lacked a standardized way to interface with modern virtual reality hardware, leaving players to rely on third-party injection tools or flat-screen viewing. The PlayStation 3 era featured several titles with stereoscopic 3D support and motion-heavy gameplay via the PlayStation Move, but without native VR integration, these features remained tethered to traditional displays. Bridging the gap between the emulator's internal rendering pipeline and the diverse ecosystem of VR headsets required a robust, cross-platform standard that could handle both high-performance video output and low-latency motion tracking.

The introduction of an OpenXR backend provides a unified solution for Windows and Linux users. OpenXR acts as a middleware layer, allowing the emulator to communicate with various runtimes like SteamVR or Monado without needing device-specific code. Technically, this implementation involves a dedicated session thread that manages an independent Vulkan device for the VR runtime. A sophisticated frame-sharing mechanism was developed to bridge the emulator's RSX graphics backends—both Vulkan and OpenGL—with the OpenXR renderer. This system uses external memory handles and semaphores to transfer rendered frames into the headset's swapchain, ensuring that the virtual display or 3D view remains synchronized with the emulator's internal frame timing.

For the player, this change introduces two primary features: immersive rendering and enhanced motion control. The emulator can now project the game onto a virtual screen within the headset or directly output stereoscopic 3D content for supported titles. Beyond visuals, the update includes an OpenXR pad handler and a specialized PlayStation Move handler. This allows VR controllers, such as those for the Quest 3, to function as direct replacements for the original PS Move hardware. By mapping the spatial data from VR controllers to the emulator's motion inputs, players can interact with motion-controlled games using the precision of modern tracking systems, significantly improving the accessibility of the PS3's motion-based library.

To utilize these new features, users must have an OpenXR-compatible runtime installed and active on their system. While the rendering backend is built on Vulkan, it is designed to work even if the emulator itself is using the OpenGL backend, thanks to the cross-API frame sharing logic. Currently, the OpenXR input configuration is handled during gameplay, and the system is optimized for headsets like the Quest 3, though the use of the OpenXR SDK ensures broad compatibility with other hardware. Developers and testers can verify the integration by checking the new OpenXR options in the I/O and Video settings, monitoring the dedicated openxr log channel for session initialization and frame-sharing status.
